What this pool service line in Yuma is, and is not

If you are looking for pool service in Yuma, AZ, this site gives you one free number to call instead of a list of companies to work through.

Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro is a phone line and a website. It is not a pool company. No one from the line will come to your yard, test your water, carry chemicals or work on your pump. What it does is answer the phone, ask you a couple of short questions about what is wrong, and hand you over to a Yuma-area pool service business with local owners and no ownership tie to the line.

Once you are connected, the arrangement is between you and that company. It looks at the pool, explains what it sees, names its own price, does the job once you approve it, and bills you itself. The call costs you nothing. Those businesses may pay the line for the referral, and every page says so.

Why a Yuma pool needs steady care

A backyard pool here deals with a mix of conditions that is hard on water and equipment. None of them is a reason to panic, but together they explain why so many owners keep a regular service schedule, and why a pool that is left alone for a few weeks in summer can change fast.

Long, very hot summers

National Weather Service figures for Yuma (1991 to 2020 normals) show that about 118 days each year reach 100 degrees or more, usually from late April into early October, and about 25 days at 110 or above. The normal July high is 106.7 degrees. Warm water lets algae grow quickly, and a pump that runs long hours in that heat wears on its seals and motor.

Strong sun all year

Visit Yuma reports that the sun shines during about 91 percent of daylight hours here. Sunlight breaks chlorine down, so outdoor pools usually carry cyanuric acid, a stabilizer that slows the sun's damage to chlorine. For water with a stabilizer in it, CDC guidance is free chlorine of 2 parts per million or more and a pH from 7.0 to 7.8.

Hard Colorado River water

The City of Yuma treats Colorado River water for its customers, and its own water FAQ calls that water hard, at 18 to 22 grains per gallon. Calcium hardness is the calcium content of the water, measured as a concentration. As pool water evaporates, its calcium stays in the pool, and each refill adds a fresh load of minerals. Over time that leaves the white crust on waterline tile and scale inside heaters and salt cells. Pool tile and calcium cleaning explains how that crust is removed.

Monsoon dust

Monsoon season, by the weather service's definition, runs from June 15 through September 30. A NOAA study names Yuma among the places where strong winds lift walls of dust, with dust storms most common in late July and early August. Dust and blown debris clog filters and use up chlorine, so the water can go cloudy within days.

Months away in summer

Many pool owners here are winter visitors. A 2017 to 2018 study for Visit Yuma estimated about 71,000 winter visitors who stayed 30 days or more between December and May, and Yuma County says its population grows by about 90,000 in winter. When those owners head north for the summer, their pools sit through the hottest months. That is often when water turns green. Yuma County Public Health calls green, unmaintained pools a major breeding source for West Nile mosquitoes. If yours has already turned, read my pool is green: how do I fix it.

Check the company before work starts

The company you reach is independent, so choosing whether to hire it is your decision. A few questions make that easier. For regular service, ask what one visit includes, how often it comes, and whether chemicals are part of the price or billed separately. Before a repair, get the price on paper and write down the license number the company holds with the Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC). Liability insurance is not a condition of an ROC license, so ask the company to show you its coverage before work begins.

Check the contractor license. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) issues the licenses for pool work. Residential R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair, is the classification for servicing a home pool and handling minor repairs. Building a new pool or putting in a whole new plaster or pebble surface falls under construction classifications such as B-5. Routine cleaning on its own is a gray area the ROC has not written a clear rule on, so simply ask the company what it holds. Then type its ROC number into the ROC contractor search (new tab) to see if the license is current, what type it is and any recent complaints. Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro does not run this lookup for you.

Common questions

Is there a pool service in Yuma AZ that answers at night?

The line itself does. An automated assistant picks up around the clock, weekends and holidays included, and tries to put you through to a local pool company. If no one at the company is free at that hour, the assistant forwards your name, phone number, community and pool problem so the company can call back. The visit time is something you settle with the company.

How much does pool service cost in Yuma?

Prices come from the pool company, never from the line, and no publisher puts out a figure for Yuma alone. National cost guides are a starting point: HomeGuide, for example, lists weekly or every-other-week cleaning service at roughly $80 to $150 a month. Your own quote will depend on the size and condition of the pool, what each visit covers and whether chemicals cost extra. The pool maintenance cost guide compares several published ranges.

Does Yuma Pool Cleaning Pro clean pools itself?

No. It is only a free phone number plus this website. It has no workers, trucks or chemicals of its own, and it does not clean, fix, price or book any pool work. It transfers you to a pool business that is locally owned and separate from the line, which does the job and bills you itself. Those businesses may pay the line for referrals.

Who will I be talking to when the call goes through?

A pool service company that is locally owned, independent of this site and works in the Yuma area. It hears a short summary of what you told the assistant before it says hello, which saves you explaining everything twice. The line does not rank or review anyone, so request the ROC license number from the company and run it through the Arizona ROC contractor search.

Can I call if I live in the Foothills, Somerton or San Luis?

Yes. The line takes calls from Yuma, Fortuna Foothills, Somerton, San Luis, Wellton and Gadsden. Mention your community to the assistant so the call goes to a company serving it. The service areas page notes the local water and power providers for each one.
